Dispersions
dis-PER-zhunz
n. plural (scatterings; the state or periods of a people being scattered among the nations)
From Latin dispergere, to scatter abroad, from dis-, apart, and spargere, to scatter, sprinkle.

Biblical Definition

Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel.

Jeremiah's oracle targets the shepherds, the political and religious leaders of Judah and the surrounding nations, pronouncing the appointed days of your slaughter and of your dispersions as accomplished, that is, as having fully come due, their measure of judgment complete. The dispersions in view are the coming exiles, the scattering of leaders and people alike among foreign lands as covenant judgment for persistent unfaithfulness, a theme Jeremiah develops at length throughout his prophecy. The vivid image, ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel, pictures something precious and finely made shattering suddenly and completely, the very leaders who should have guarded the flock becoming instead broken pottery scattered among the nations. Jeremiah's larger prophetic ministry holds this severe judgment together with genuine hope of future restoration (Jer 29:10-14; 31:31-34), a pattern of discipline followed by covenant renewal that the dictionary traces throughout Israel's history as the LORD's consistent dealing with his covenant people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from DISPERSE: the act or state of being scattered abroad; a scattering of a people among various places or nations.

DISPERSE, v.t. To scatter in different directions; to spread abroad.

DISPERSION, n. The act or state of being scattered; a scattering abroad.

Jeremiah 25: Judah's shepherds face appointed days of dispersions.

Pictures a precious vessel shattering suddenly and completely.

Held together with genuine hope of future covenant restoration.

Key Scripture

Jer 25:34 — "Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel."

Modern Corruption

Reading the exile purely as a geopolitical misfortune, detached from Jeremiah's own insistence that it is covenant discipline for unfaithfulness, strips the dispersions of their actual theological meaning.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation here is historical-critical minimalism, treating the Babylonian exile as mere ancient power politics with no covenantal significance.

The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own repeated framing: the dispersions are the LORD's appointed judgment on unfaithful shepherds and people (Jer 25:4-7), discipline measured out in holiness, not accident, and held together throughout the book with the LORD's unbroken promise of eventual restoration and a new covenant (Jer 31:31-34).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin dispergere compounds dis-, apart, with spargere, to scatter or sprinkle — dispersion names a scattering apart, the same root that gives the later technical term diaspora for Israel's scattering among the nations.

expand to see more

Dis-, apart, and spargere, to scatter, form dispergere.

Dispersion names a scattering apart among many places.

Jeremiah applies it to the coming exile of Judah's leaders.

Pictures a precious vessel shattering suddenly and completely.

Held together with the LORD's promise of future restoration.
